messages.subject: JOB: Post-Doctoral position (animal abundance) in Italy
messages.subject_clean: JOB: Post-Doctoral position (animal abundance) in Italy
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance-sampling list:

I'm passing on information about a possible post-doc position in applied
estimation of animal abundance (below).  Please contact Neil Walker
<n.wa...@csl.gov.uk> for details.

 - Len

==================BEGIN FORWARDED MESSAGE==================

> >A quick introduction - I work as on-site Stato at Woodchester Park
> >Research Station, which is the site of a long-term capture-recapture
> >survey on a wild badger population. I'm writing with respect to an
> >upcoming Post-Doc position and to see if there is anyone in your
> >department who would be interested in applying.

> >The last year has seen the start of a collaboration between
> >ourselves (the Wildlife Disease Ecology Team of the Central Science
> >Laboratory) and the Institute of Alpine Ecology, Trento, Italy. Our
> >colleague Dr Francesca Cagnacci is carrying out a project at the
> >Institute on the Epidemiology of tick-borne diseases in the Italian
> >Alps.
> >The relevant regional authority in Italy (Trentino) will fund a
> >Post-Doc position to design sampling strategies for estimating
> >animal abundance at different spatial scales and to analyse the
> >arising data.

> >Key elements include:
> >-    Estimating abundance of deer and voles (both hosts in the cycle
> >of tick transmission). Data will be collected at different spatial
> >scales for the respective species.  Distance sampling methodology
> >and trapping webs are likely to be employed.
> >-    Investigating different abundance estimation techniques in
> >light of above point re:different spatial scales

> >This will be for the most part desk-based work. Some field work in
> >Italy will be involved - accommodation for these visits will be
> >provided free of charge by the Institute in Trento. CSL will be
> >involved in aspects of Study Design and advising on data collection
> >in the field. Obviously, this would suit someone with a PhD or soon
> >to finish with a strong background in population modelling and some
> >grounding in spatial analysis.

> >Francesca is currently finishing writing up a formal proposal - I
> >have attached the latest version which has all the key details.

[I haven't forwarded this attachment -- please contact Neil Walker if
interested - LJT]

messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

I would like to use MCDS to analyze the effect of different observers in
detection probabilities but I still don't understand the required data
format.
In the on-line manual there is this example for data format in MCDS:

Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      14
Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      8
Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      22
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    7
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    37
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    13
Stratum B      123     Line 1B 5.7
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     27
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     76
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     44
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     7

This look like a CDS (Conventional Distance Sampling) format.
How can I include a covariate in Distance?
Thank you very much in advance.
Best,

Manuel

messages.subject: Re: MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Manuel, list,

I believe the example you sent, which I found on page 47 of the Distance=20
5 User Manual, is not referring to MCDS but to CDS. Maybe I missed it,=20
but I have not seen any reference in the manual indicating it to be=20
MCDS, it's just an example data set, in this instance, a CDS one.

The simplest way to include covariates is just to add a column for each=20
variable to a standard data file format, with the corresponding=20
covariate value in front of each observed distance. Using the example=20
data set you sent, and assuming a covariate sex =3D (male,M or female,F)=20
and a covariate age =3D(1,2,3), an example data set would look like

Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      14	F	1
Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      8	F	1=09
Stratum A      100     Line 1A 10      22	M	3
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    7	F	2
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    37	M	1
Stratum A      100     Line 2A 10.3    13	F	3
Stratum B      123     Line 1B 5.7    =20
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     27	F	1
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     76	M	2
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     44	M	2
Stratum B      123     Line 2B 8.4     7	F	1

The importing of the data should not be much more complicated than=20
without covariates, you just have to define the covariate names=20
appropriately.

Remember if you code a covariate with numbers, but the covariate is to=20
be used as a factor  (say sex 0 and 1 instead of M and F) you need to=20
tell distance that it should analyse this variable as a factor by=20
ticking the factor box in the model definition | detection function |=20
covariates tab, and also tick the apropriate box if the covariate is=20
cluster size.

Hope this makes it easyer,

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.subject: Adjusting raw counts with Distance-derived prob. of detect.
messages.subject_clean: Adjusting raw counts with Distance-derived prob. of detect.
messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

I'm hoping to get some feedback on my proposed method for adjusting raw
abundance counts (a.k.a. relative abundance) with Distance-derived
probabilities of detection.  I am doing a study of forest landbird
communities at 75 sites along an urbanization gradient.  I conducted
point transects at these sites (5 stations per site, visited 3 times
each), placing detections into the following distance intervals: 0-25 m,
25-50 m, 50-75 m, and 75-100 m.  I am happy to defend my use of
intervals, but it's not really relevant here.  Ultimately, I want to
have site-specific counts of all species that I can use as dependent
variables in multiple regressions and other analyses.

I wish to use program Distance to adjust the raw counts of birds.  I
cannot do this on a site-by-site basis, except perhaps for all species
combined, because of a low number of detections.  (The total number of
bird detections of all species per site across all visits to all
stations averaged about 314 birds.)  I thought, however, that I could
put sites into urbanization categories (strata) and calculate
stratum-specific probabilities of detection with which to adjust the raw
counts (or more likely, the average count across 3 visits and 5
stations) at each site.  The use of separate detection functions for
urbanization categories makes sense to me, as noise levels, which often
interfere with my mostly auditory detections, increase with
urbanization.  So I placed the sites in 6 categories of urbanization
(low to high), calculated species-specific probabilities of detection
for each category, and then adjusted counts of each species at each site
by dividing them by the probability of detection for that site's
category.  I might use 3 urbanization categories for some species if I
don't have enough observations to get a reliable probability of
detection using 6 categories, and possibly use a global probability of
detection for species that still have too few observations.  One
potential problem with this approach, if I understand correctly, is that
the estimates within a development class will not be independent because
they were derived from the same detection function.  I don't know how
much of a problem this is.

I have done some preliminary analyses, with mixed results.  It seems
difficult to get a reliable detection function.  There is rarely a
"shoulder," as I'm working with four intervals and the probability of
detection nearly always drops off quickly after the first category.
Still, the goodness-of-fit tests and the CVs seem okay.  Second, nearly
all the probabilities of detection for the highest development category
are in the neighborhood of 0.10 - 0.15.  When I adjust the raw counts,
this yields abundance values that are 6x-10x the raw counts.  Some of
the adjusted values seem way too high, based on years of experience
counting birds in this area.  Forty-five jays on average at a single
point transect?  No way.  Further, some of the probability of detection
values are absurdly low.  Finally, zero values are unadjusted by this
method, but zero values could actually represent undetected birds.
Incidentally, I likely have similar problems to those discussed in
mid-April on this listserve: counting more than singing males, and
problems with the "snapshot" assumption. =20

I could use various types of advice.  What do you think of this approach
over all?  Is there a better way?  Essentially, how can one use Distance
to calculate site-specific abundances when there are not enough
detections at each site to model site-specific detection functions?  Can
I somehow use covariate distance sampling, with which I am only vaguely
familiar, to yield better adjusted values?  Is there any way I can end
up with better detection functions and therefore more reasonable
probability of detection estimates?

Thanks for reading my book.  I look forward to any advice.

Matt
 =20

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Matthew Schlesinger
Dept. of Environmental Science and Policy
University of California, Davis
One Shields Avenue
Davis, CA 95616
(530) 752-2843
mdschl...@ucdavis.edu
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

messages.subject: Re: Adjusting raw counts with Distance-derived prob. of detect.
messages.subject_clean: Adjusting raw counts with Distance-derived prob. of detect.
messages.body_plain:
Matt, a few brief thoughts.  Overall, your strategy seems fine.  A
different strategy that you might consider is to use a measure of
urbanization as a covariate, and use multiple covariate distance sampling,
which is in current versions of Distance.  This reduces the problems due
to small sample sizes.

It sounds like there is some problem with the data, with too many
detections in the first interval, especially in the most urbanized
stratum.  I wonder if this might be related to the impossibility of
locating points at random in an urban environment?  Perhaps habitat close
to the point tends to have a higher density of birds?  Also in an urban
environment, might your jays tend to approach the observer, so be recorded
too close?  By collecting interval data, it is more difficult to ensure
that you get a good model fit.  I suspect default model selection in
Distance is selecting implausible model shapes, due to some feature of the
data.  I would be inclined to stick with say the half-normal model with no
adjustment terms, to try to get a more robust analysis.  (I would however
include a measure of urbanization as a covariate in the half-normal
detection fn.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: comparing density estimates
messages.body_plain:
I have explored the list archives as well as the manual and intro book. At
this point, it might just suffice to pose my question to the listserv...

My question is based on how to proceed after density estimates are obtained.
For instance, in my point count data, I stratified on 5 different areas (5
different distances from development) and obtained density estimates for a
bird species in those 5 different areas; I then have 5 D's, with each its own
df, SE, CV, etc., as well as a pooled value - which is not of as much concern
to me. I want to determine if 1 D in 1 area significantly differs from another
D or group of Ds, etc. in another area(s).

It seems that as per p. 84 of Intro to Distance Sampling, I can determine var
of D1 and D2 by squaring the SE of D1 and D2. Then, to get var(D1-D2)...
varD1+varD2.  Then, manually caluculate a Z-value: (D1-D2) / square root of
var(D1-D2).  That gives a Z-value, which can then be compared to critical
values in a z-table at a specified significance level. Is that correct?

It seems that ANOVAs can also be performed?

However, as per the last inquiry to the listserv, Matt states "One potential
problem with this approach, if I understand correctly, is that the estimates
within a development class will not be independent because they were derived
from the same detection function. I don't know how much of a problem this is."
Would that apply in my case as well?

Thank you very much for anyone's assistance--
Elena

--

messages.subject: Re: comparing density estimates
messages.body_plain:
If you have used data pooled across strata to estimate the detection
function, then you can't assume that stratum densities are independent.
This is addressed on p85 of the 2001 intro to DS book.

If you have just one density estimate per stratum, ANOVA on the stratum
density estimates won't work, as you don't have within-stratum
replication.  If you are prepared to assume a common detection function
across strata, an option is to do a (weighted) ANOVA of line-specific
encounter rates.

Steve Buckland
